newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Buenos Aires governor lashes out over bank.
newsitem.headline: Buenos Aires governor lashes out over bank.

text.p: The Governor of Buenos Aires Province and Peronist presidential candidate for 1999, Eduardo Duhalde, lashed out at Argentine bankers Tuesday for instisting he must privatize the province's bank.

Duhalde, second-in-command of the ruling Peronist Party and former deputy of President Carlos Menem, is accused by top bankers of "treading an opposite path to Menem" by failing to embrace whole-heartedly free-market economic reforms.

"They want to get their hands on the bank," Duhalde told local radio, calling their campaign for the privatization of Banco de la Provincia de Buenos Aires "ridiculous" and inspired by fear of competition.

Banco Provincia is Argentina's second biggest bank, after the state-run Banco Nacion, in terms of volume of deposits and loans. It is also a major player in private pension funds and labor insurance with private-sector partners.
Private sector bankers complain that Banco Provincia has unfair competitive advantages in the marketplace such as its exemption from taxes, including value added tax.
"We want the same rules of the game for everyone," said Julio Gomez, head of the foreign banks' lobby ABRA.

The debate over the Banco Provincia has been simmering for a long time, with smaller enterprises and the powerful farm lobby demanding that it remain in state hands because it is a major source of low-cost financing.

But the debate erupted on to the front pages of the press this weekend when Eduardo Escasany, head of the Association of Argentine Banks and president of Banco de Galicia, accused Duhalde of "old-style Peronist attitudes."

"He doesn't believe in the private sector and he sends contradictory messages on the role of the state. Duhalde is moving in the opposite direction to President Carlos Menem's reforms... If he gets his way he will touch the spinal cord of this change Argentina has gone through," said Escasany.
Such criticisms are frequently levelled at Duhalde, who questions the social impact of the wholesale privatizations and free-market reform espoused by Menem.

The issue is especially sensitive in an election year, when Duhalde hopes to boost his already considerable sway over the Peronist structure in the mid-term elections in Congress scheduled for October.
The governor accused the private-sector bankers of "not knowing what the bank means for businessmen, cooperatives and the people of the interior."

"Only the Provincia will help out when things get really difficult...not by throwing money at people, but by showing the friendly face of an institution that is not only about business," said Duhalde.
